clinicalPearls: A syndrome of bleeding into the alveoli from the pulmonary microcirculation, not a single disease
Classic features are haemoptysis, diffuse alveolar infiltrates, anaemia and hypoxaemia, though haemoptysis can be absent
A falling haemoglobin with new alveolar shadowing should raise the possibility even without haemoptysis
Sequential bronchoalveolar lavage returning progressively bloodier aliquots confirms alveolar haemorrhage
Causes include small-vessel vasculitis, anti-GBM disease, connective tissue disease, drugs and coagulopathy, grouped by the presence or absence of capillaritis
Management combines supportive care with urgent immunosuppression when an immune cause is identified
reference.pathophysiology: Diffuse alveolar haemorrhage arises from disruption of the alveolar-capillary basement membrane, allowing red cells to enter the alveolar spaces. The commonest mechanism is pulmonary capillaritis, a neutrophilic inflammation of the microvasculature seen in small-vessel vasculitides and connective tissue disease. Other cases result from bland haemorrhage without inflammation (as in coagulopathy or raised pulmonary venous pressure) or from diffuse alveolar damage. Accumulated blood impairs gas exchange, and recurrent bleeding can lead to haemosiderosis and fibrosis.
additionalInvestigations: Sequential bronchoalveolar lavage demonstrating persistent or increasing blood
Chest imaging and full blood count for anaemia
Autoimmune serology (ANCA, anti-GBM, ANA and others)
Renal assessment for a pulmonary-renal syndrome
Coagulation studies and echocardiography as indicated
reference.prognosis: Prognosis depends on the cause and speed of treatment; immune capillaritis can respond well to prompt immunosuppression, but delayed treatment or severe disease carries significant mortality.
pitfalls: Excluding the diagnosis because haemoptysis is absent
Mistaking it for infection or pulmonary oedema and delaying immunosuppression
Failing to identify a treatable immune cause
